title: Coding Practice: Hoisting & Scope
description: Six short snippets that expose exactly how var, let, and function declarations are hoisted and scoped.

blocks.title: 1. var Hoisting
blocks.question: What is the output, and why?
blocks.explanation: var declarations are hoisted to the top of their function/global scope and initialized to undefined before any code runs — only the declaration is hoisted, not the assignment. The first log sees the hoisted-but-unassigned variable; by the second log the assignment on line 3 has run.
hints: Hoisting splits a `var` declaration from its assignment.
No error is thrown here — that's the giveaway it isn't let/const.

blocks.title: 2. let and the Temporal Dead Zone
blocks.question: undefined or error? Why?
blocks.code:
console.log(a);

let a = 10;
blocks.explanation: let (and const) are hoisted to the top of the block too, but they are not initialized — they sit in the Temporal Dead Zone from the start of the block until their declaration line executes. Reading them before that line throws, unlike var's silent undefined.
hints: Compare this directly against snippet 1 — same shape, different keyword, different failure mode.

blocks.title: 3. Function Declaration Hoisting
blocks.question: Does this work?
blocks.explanation: Function declarations (unlike function expressions) are hoisted completely, body included, so the function is fully callable before its position in the source text.

blocks.title: 4. Function Expression Hoisting
blocks.question: What happens here?
blocks.answer: TypeError: sayHello is not a function.
blocks.explanation: Only the `var sayHello` declaration is hoisted (initialized to undefined) — the function assignment happens at the line where it's written. At the point of the call, sayHello is still undefined, and calling undefined() throws a TypeError, not a ReferenceError. That distinction (TypeError vs ReferenceError) is exactly what interviewers listen for.
hints: This is a different error type than snippet 2 — say why out loud.

blocks.title: 5. var Is Function-Scoped
blocks.question: Can name be accessed outside the if block?
blocks.explanation: var ignores block boundaries (`if`, `for`, `while`) entirely; it is scoped to the nearest enclosing function (or the global scope). The if block does not create a new scope for var.

blocks.title: 6. let Is Block-Scoped
blocks.question: What happens when var is replaced with let?
blocks.explanation: let is scoped to the block it's declared in — the `{ }` of the if statement — so it simply does not exist once execution leaves that block. This pair (5 and 6) is the cleanest possible illustration of function-scope vs block-scope.

title: Coding Practice: Closures
description: Four snippets that build up closure intuition, ending in the classic var-vs-let loop interview question.

blocks.title: 7. A Basic Closure
blocks.question: What's the output, and why doesn't count reset between calls?
blocks.explanation: inner() closes over the `count` variable from outer()'s scope. Each call to outer() would create a brand-new `count`, but here outer() only runs once — counter always refers to that same single `count` binding, which is why it keeps incrementing instead of resetting.

blocks.title: 8. Two Independent Closures
blocks.question: Predict all four logged values.
blocks.explanation: counter1 and counter2 come from two separate invocations of createCounter(), so each gets its own private `count` in its own closure. counter2's calls never touch counter1's count, which is why counter2() resets to 1 while counter1 keeps climbing to 3.

blocks.title: 9. var Inside a Loop with setTimeout
blocks.question: Is the output 0 1 2, or something else? Explain using closures.
blocks.explanation: There is only one `i` for the whole loop (var is function/global-scoped), and all three callbacks close over that same binding. By the time any setTimeout callback actually runs — after the synchronous loop has fully finished — `i` has already reached 3, so every callback logs the same final value.
hints: This is the single most common JavaScript interview question — make sure you can explain the fix, not just the output.

blocks.title: 10. let Inside a Loop with setTimeout
blocks.question: Why is this different from the previous example?
blocks.explanation: let creates a brand-new binding of `i` for every single iteration of the loop, and each setTimeout callback closes over its own iteration's binding. That's why switching var to let is the standard one-line fix for the previous snippet's bug.

title: Coding Practice: References, Destructuring, Rest & Spread
description: Object reference semantics, the shallow-copy trap, and the destructuring/rest/spread syntax that comes up in almost every interview.

blocks.title: 11. Object Reference Assignment
blocks.question: Why does changing user2 affect user1?
blocks.explanation: Objects are assigned and passed by reference. `const user2 = user1` copies the reference (the memory address), not the object itself — user1 and user2 point at the exact same object, so mutating through either name reads back on both.

blocks.title: 12. Shallow Copy with Spread
blocks.question: Why does spread fix the top-level change but not the nested one?
blocks.explanation: `{ ...user1 }` copies only the top-level properties into a new object — `name` becomes an independent string value, so reassigning user2.name never touches user1. But `address` is copied as a reference, not deep-cloned, so user1.address and user2.address still point to the identical nested object; mutating city through either one is visible on both.
hints: To fix this you need a deep clone: structuredClone(user1), or a nested spread { ...user1, address: { ...user1.address } }.

blocks.title: 13. Destructuring with Renaming
blocks.question: Given the object below, destructure `name` into a variable called `userName` while still pulling out `city` normally.
blocks.explanation: The `oldName: newName` syntax inside a destructuring pattern renames the binding on the left while still reading the property named on the right from the source object.

blocks.title: 14. Rest Operator in Array Destructuring
blocks.question: What is inside remaining?
blocks.explanation: The rest element (`...remaining`) must come last in the pattern and collects every element not already picked off individually, into a real array — not a reference into the original array.

blocks.title: 15. Spread Operator: Inserting a Value Mid-Array
blocks.question: Modify the code so result is [1, 2, 3, 100, 4, 5, 6].
blocks.explanation: Spread just splices an iterable's elements in wherever it appears in the array literal — placing a literal value between two spreads inserts it exactly at that position, no concat() or splice() needed.

title: Coding Practice: map, filter & reduce
description: The three array methods that show up in nearly every practical JavaScript interview exercise.

blocks.title: 16. Does map() Mutate the Original Array?
blocks.question: Does map() modify the original array?
blocks.explanation: map() is non-mutating — it always returns a brand-new array built from the callback's return values, leaving the original array untouched. This is exactly why map()/filter()/reduce() compose so well: each one hands the next a fresh array.

blocks.title: 17. filter() Employees by Salary
blocks.question: Using filter(), return only the employees whose salary is greater than 50000.
blocks.answer:
const result = employees.filter(emp => emp.salary > 50000);
// [{ name: "B", salary: 70000 }, { name: "C", salary: 90000 }]
blocks.explanation: filter() keeps only the elements for which the predicate callback returns a truthy value, and — like map() — returns a new array without touching the original.

blocks.title: 18. reduce() to Sum an Array
blocks.question: Using reduce(), calculate the total of [10, 20, 30, 40]. Then explain what `acc` and `current` are in reduce((acc, current) => {}, 0).
blocks.code: const numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40];
blocks.answer:
const total = numbers.reduce((acc, current) => acc + current, 0);
// total === 100
blocks.explanation: `acc` (the accumulator) carries the running result from one iteration to the next — it starts as the second argument to reduce() (here, 0) and becomes whatever the callback returned on the previous step. `current` is simply the array element being visited on this iteration. reduce() is the most general array method: map() and filter() can both be implemented in terms of it.

blocks.title: 19. Combine filter() and map()
blocks.question: From [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], produce only the even numbers, each multiplied by 10 — using filter() then map().
blocks.code: const numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6];
blocks.explanation: Chaining filter() then map() reads as a pipeline: first narrow down to the elements you care about, then transform each surviving element. Doing it in the opposite order (map then filter) also works here, but filter-then-map is usually cheaper since map only ever runs on the elements that passed the filter.

title: Coding Practice: this, call/apply/bind, Promises & the Event Loop
description: Five snippets covering the most senior-heavy JavaScript interview territory: this-binding and asynchronous execution order.

blocks.title: 20. Regular Method vs Arrow Method
blocks.question: Why can arrow functions behave differently with this? Compare the two versions of printName.
blocks.explanation: userA.printName is a regular (shorthand) method, so `this` is determined by the call site: `userA.printName()` sets `this` to userA, and this.name is "Roshan". Arrow functions never bind their own `this` — they capture it lexically from where they were *defined*, which here is the top level of the module, not the object literal. So userB.printName's `this` is whatever `this` is outside the object (undefined in a module/strict/class context), and this.name is undefined — the object literal `{ name: ... }` is never consulted at all.
hints: The fix for real code that needs `this` to be the enclosing object is: never use an arrow function for an object method that reads `this`.

blocks.title: 21. call(), apply(), and bind()
blocks.question: Call introduce with this bound to `user` using call(), apply(), and bind(). What's the difference between the three?
blocks.explanation: All three explicitly set `this` for introduce, but they differ in invocation: call() invokes immediately with arguments passed individually; apply() invokes immediately with arguments passed as a single array; bind() does not invoke at all — it returns a brand-new function permanently bound to the given `this` (and optionally partial arguments), which you call later. bind() is the one to reach for when a callback is handed off to code you don't control (event listeners, setTimeout) and needs to keep its `this`.

blocks.title: 22. Promise Executor Timing
blocks.question: Predict the exact order of the four logs.
blocks.explanation: The Promise executor function runs synchronously and immediately when `new Promise(...)` is called — that's why "Promise" logs before "End", not after. Calling resolve() only schedules the .then() callback as a microtask; it can't run until the current synchronous block finishes, so "End" still logs before "Success".

blocks.title: 23. The Event Loop: setTimeout vs Promise
blocks.question: Predict the order of A, B, C, D. Explain using the call stack, Web APIs, the microtask queue, the macrotask queue, and the event loop.
blocks.explanation: "A" and "D" run synchronously on the call stack first. setTimeout hands its callback off to the Web API/timer facility, which queues it as a macrotask only once the delay elapses — even a 0ms delay still waits for the current script to finish. Promise.resolve().then() queues its callback as a microtask instead. After every synchronous statement finishes, the event loop always drains the entire microtask queue ("C") before pulling a single task from the macrotask queue ("B").
hints: Microtasks (Promises, queueMicrotask) always fully drain before the next macrotask (setTimeout, setInterval, I/O) runs — no exceptions.

blocks.title: 24. async/await Execution Order
blocks.question: Predict the output order of 1, 2, 3, 4.
blocks.explanation: "3" logs first since it's the next synchronous line. Calling test() runs its body synchronously up to the first `await` — logging "1" — then the await suspends the async function and immediately returns control to the caller, so "4" logs next. Only after the current synchronous script finishes does the microtask resuming test() run, logging "2" last. async/await is syntax sugar over exactly the Promise-then microtask behavior from the previous two snippets.

title: Coding Practice: Real-World Data Transformation
description: A senior-level capstone problem: reshaping a flat array into a grouped lookup object using reduce().

blocks.title: 25. Group Employees by Department
blocks.question: Convert this flat array of employees into an object keyed by department, where each key maps to the array of employees in that department. Solve it using reduce().
blocks.explanation: This is the general "group-by" pattern built on reduce(): the accumulator starts as an empty object; on each element, look up (or lazily create with `??=`) the array for that element's key, and push the element into it. It's one of the most commonly asked practical JavaScript exercises because it combines object/array manipulation, reduce mechanics, and real data-shaping in one problem.
hints: A natural follow-up: also compute just the *count* of employees per department instead of the full arrays — same pattern, `acc[key] = (acc[key] ?? 0) + 1`.
